rv.q: It’s thrilling that a production about youth gathers strength from the authentic and ongoing experience of those making the show.
Amid the warmth and humor of her portrait of teenagehood, Smith is touching on a cold and bracing thing.
Dad Don’t Read This is tender, piercing, and deeply human.

A work of shocking, thrilling intimacy, Dad Don’t Read This invites the audience to slip on their pajamas and revel in the freedom, and anxiety-ridden constraint, of youth as it haphazrdly transforms.
What makes Smith’s writing especially satisfying is how she never succumbs to the urge to turn any of that subtext into text.
Smith compassionately documents the young ladies’ attempts at forging their own life stories and being kind to each other while surrounded by gossip and peer pressure.
Eliya Smith's play about four teenaged girls is raw and messy and heartbreaking and joyful all at once.
That said, Dad Don’t Read This is highly entertaining and Smith impresses as a playwright ready to break through.
Throughout, Smith has an uncanny knack for getting inside her characters' heads, anatomizing their dreams, fantasies, and fears.
Although the play is completely authentic and persuasive, as it is plotless we do not know where it is going.

For Dad Don’t Read This, directed by Chloe Claudel, the cast of four acquit themselves with guts and honesty (and good humor) but are caught in the web of a sticky storyline that spins itself without going nowhere.

cn.t: Smith's sharp, immersive portrait of teenage girls at sleepovers earns praise for its raw authenticity and emotional depth, though some critics find it struggles to distinguish itself in a crowded field of similar adolescent dramas.
